Only after initial IV volume restoration; otherwise the gut may not absorb fluids.
faq.q: Can oral rehydration be used in shock?

faq.a: When there is ongoing haemorrhage with Hb < 7 g/dL or signs of inadequate oxygen delivery despite fluids.

exam: What is the first bedside step in a child with suspected hypovolaemic shock? — Assess capillary refill, mental status and start a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus.
How does you differentiate hypovolaemic from septic shock in a febrile child? — Cold, clammy skin and low pulse pressure point to hypovolaemia; warm skin and bounding pulse suggest septic shock.
A child with severe diarrhoea is hypotensive after 40 mL/kg fluids. What next? — Look for ongoing loss, give a second bolus, and start oral rehydration once perfusion improves.
Why are colloids avoided in malaria‑related shock? — Capillary leak increases risk of pulmonary oedema and worsens outcomes.
What laboratory test would you request if available, and what would a high lactate indicate? — Serum lactate; > 2 mmol/L suggests tissue hypoxia and severe shock.

Explain why a child with a head injury and hypovolaemic shock needs a different fluid strategy than an isolated dehydration case. — Maintain cerebral perfusion pressure; avoid rapid over‑resuscitation that raises intracranial pressure.
When is blood transfusion indicated in paediatric hypovolaemic shock? — Ongoing haemorrhage with Hb < 7 g/dL or signs of inadequate oxygen delivery despite fluids.
What red‑flag sign would make you call for urgent surgical assistance? — Persistent uncontrolled external bleeding or expanding abdominal distension indicating intra‑abdominal haemorrhage.
ai.title: Hypovolaemic Shock in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Hypovolaemic shock is a life‑threatening state of inadequate circulating volume causing tissue hypoperfusion. In low‑resource settings it often follows severe dehydration, haemorrhage or third‑spacing. Prompt recognition, rapid fluid resuscitation and treatment of the underlying cause are essential.

b: Systolic BP <5th percentile for age or >20% drop from baseline
Capillary refill >2 seconds
Cold, clammy skin
sections.p: A reversible circulatory failure due to a fall in intravascular volume that leads to insufficient oxygen delivery to tissues.

t.b: Is perfusion adequate? – Low systolic or MAP < (2 × age + 70) mmHg suggests shock.
Is peripheral perfusion compromised? – >2 seconds supports shock.
Is renal perfusion adequate? – <1 mL/kg/h indicates severe hypoperfusion.

b: Stage I (compensated): tachycardia, normal BP, delayed cap refill
Stage II (moderate): tachycardia, systolic BP 70‑80 mmHg, oliguria
Stage III (severe): hypotension, cold extremities, altered mental status
sections.p: The WHO/PAHO classification uses clinical signs to grade shock severity.

b: Acute diarrhoea with vomiting (cholera, rotavirus)
Severe malaria with sequestration and fever‑induced sweating
Traumatic haemorrhage (road‑traffic injuries, falls)
Post‑operative bleeding or surgical loss
Burns with fluid loss
Third‑spacing from severe pancreatitis or intestinal obstruction
sections.p: In East African paediatrics the common precipitants are:

b: Tachycardia (age‑appropriate > 2 SD above mean)
Peripheral vasoconstriction – mottled or pale skin
Decreased urine output
Altered consciousness if severe
sections.p: Children look ill, irritable or lethargic, with a rapid weak pulse, cool extremities, and a dry mucous membrane.
Use bedside tools first; laboratory tests are adjuncts and may be unavailable.

t.b: Is there haemorrhagic loss? – Low Hb (< 8 g/dL) suggests bleeding.
Are there dehydration‑related derangements? – High Na⁺ (> 145 mmol/L) indicates water loss.
Is hypoglycaemia contributing? – < 2.5 mmol/L needs immediate correction.

b: Persistent hypotension after 30 min of fluid bolus
Deteriorating mental status
Acute kidney injury (urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h)
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
sections.p: Failure to restore perfusion quickly leads to irreversible organ injury.

b: Give isotonic crystalloid (0.9 % saline or Ringer's lactate) 20 mL/kg over 5‑10 min; repeat until perfusion improves.
If haemorrhage suspected, control bleeding surgically or with pressure dressings.
Treat malaria with parenteral artesunate; give antidiarrhoeal rehydration (ORS) after initial IV fluids.
Avoid colloids in children with severe infection or malaria due to risk of capillary leak.
sections.p: Rapid, controlled fluid replacement and treatment of the underlying cause are the cornerstones.

t.b: Will perfusion improve? – Rising BP, improved cap refill, increased urine output indicates response.
Is there significant blood loss? – Hb < 7 g/dL with ongoing bleed warrants transfusion.

b: Continue oral rehydration once stable; educate caregivers on ORS use.
Vaccinate against rotavirus, cholera and malaria prophylaxis where feasible.
Teach safe wound care and early presentation for trauma.
sections.p: After stabilisation monitor for rebound hypovolaemia and address the precipitating condition.

b: Septic shock – warm extremities early, fever, high cardiac output
Cardiac tamponade – muffled heart sounds, JVD, pulsus paradoxus
Anaphylactic shock – urticaria, bronchospasm, rapid onset after allergen
Normal BP in early compensated shock – rely on cap refill and mental status.
Low haemoglobin may be masked by dehydration; repeat after fluid resuscitation.
Serum lactate may be unavailable; use clinical trend of perfusion instead.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent hypotension despite two fluid boluses
Severe bleeding that cannot be controlled
